source_text:
Tunc Octauius ait: Non boni uiri est, Marce frater, hominem domi forisque lateri tuo inhaerentem sic m hac inperitiae uulgaris caecitate deserere, ut tam luculento die in lapides eum patiaris inpingere, effigiatos sane et unctos et coronatos, cum scias huius erroris non minorem ad te quam ad ipsum infamiam redundare.
cum hoc sermone eius medium spatium civitatis emensi iam liberum litus tenebamus.
ibi harenas extimas, uelut sterneret ambulacro, perfundens lenis unda tendebat, et ut semper mare etiam positis flatibus inquietum est, etsi non canis spumosisque fluctibus exibat ad terram, tamen crispis tortuosisque ibidem erroribus delectati perquam sumus, cum in ipso aequoris limine plantas tingueremus, quod uicissim nunc adpulsum nostris pedibus adluderet fluctus, nunc relabens ac uestigia retrahens in sese resorberet.
sensim itaque tranquilleque progressi oram curui molliter litoris iter fabulis fallentibus legebamus. hae fabulae erant Octaui disserentis de nauigatione narratio.
sed ubi eundi spatium satis iustum cum sermone consumpsimus, eandem emensi uiam rursus uersis uestigiis terebamus, et cum ad id loci uentum est, ubi subductae nauiculae substratis roboribus a terrena labe suspensae quiescebant, pueros uidimus certatim gestientes testarum in mare iaculationibus ludere.
is lusus est testam teretem iactatione fluctuum leuigatam legere de litore, eam testam plano situ digitis conprehensam inclinem ipsum atque humilem quantum potest super undas inrotare, ut illud iaculum uel dorsum maris raderet [uel enataret], dum leni impetu labitur, uel summis fluctibus tonsis emicaret [emergeret, dum adsiduo saltu subleuatur. is se in pueris uictorem ferebat, cuius testa et procurreret longius et frequentius exsiliret.
thought_title: Octavius rebukes Marcus for leaving Caecilius in vulgar ignorance
orientation: Octavius speaks to Marcus, the narrator, after Caecilius has kissed an idol of Serapis, and the three friends continue walking to the shore.
pass_a_gloss: Then Octavius said: It is not the part of a good man, brother Marcus, to desert a man clinging to your side at home and abroad in this blindness of vulgar ignorance, so that on so bright a day you allow him to dash against stones, stones that are shaped into images and anointed and crowned, since you know that the disgrace of this error redounds to you no less than to him. With this speech of his, having traversed the middle space of the city, we were already holding the open shore. There a gentle wave, as if it were spreading a carpet for walking, stretched over the outermost sands, and as the sea is always restless even when the winds are still, even if it did not come out to the land with white and foaming waves, nevertheless we were exceedingly delighted by its rippling and winding wanderings in that same place, when at the very edge of the water we dipped our feet, because the wave in turn now, having been driven up, played against our feet, now flowing back and drawing back our footprints, sucked them into itself. And so, having advanced slowly and quietly, we traced the path of the curving shore, softly, with stories beguiling the way. These stories were Octavius's account, discoursing about navigation. But when we had consumed a sufficiently proper space of walking with conversation, having measured out the same way, we were treading it back again with reversed steps, and when it was come to that place where small ships, drawn up on supporting timbers, were resting, raised up from the earthly dirt, we saw boys eagerly vying to play with throws of potsherds into the sea. This game is to pick from the shore a potsherd made smooth by the tossing of the waves, to grasp that potsherd with the fingers in a flat position, and to whirl it, tilted and as low as possible, over the waves, so that that missile either grazed the back of the sea or swam out, while it glided with gentle force, or darted up over the shorn tops of the waves or emerged, while it was lifted up by constant leaping. That boy was declaring himself the victor among the boys whose potsherd both ran forward farther and leaped out more frequently.

choices.why: Keeps the genitive chain and the force of 'uulgaris' as belonging to the common crowd, matching the earlier 'superstitious crowd'.

choices.english: you allow him to dash against stones
choices.why: Preserves the physical violence of 'inpingere' and the accusative 'lapides' as the object struck, not a metaphor for stumbling.
rejected: you let him stumble on stones
you suffer him to strike stones

choices.term: effigiatos sane et unctos et coronatos
choices.english: stones that are shaped into images and anointed and crowned
choices.why: Keeps the three participles as parallel descriptions of the stones, with 'sane' rendered as a concessive aside.
rejected: indeed carved and anointed and crowned
shaped, anointed, and crowned as they are

choices.english: as if it were spreading a carpet for walking
choices.why: Renders the simile with 'ambulacro' as a dative of purpose, keeping the image of the wave preparing the sand.
rejected: as if it were laying a walkway

choices.english: rippling and winding wanderings in that same place
choices.why: Keeps the double adjective and the word 'erroribus' as wanderings, preserving the playful sense of the water's movement.

choices.english: we traced the path with stories beguiling the way
choices.why: Keeps 'fallentibus' as beguiling or deceiving, and 'legebamus' as tracing or picking out the path, preserving the wordplay of reading the shore.
rejected: we read the way with deceiving stories
we beguiled the journey with tales

pass_b_english: Then Octavius said: "It is not the mark of a good man, my brother Marcus, to abandon a friend who clings to your side at home and abroad in such blindness of vulgar ignorance, and on so bright a day to allow him to dash against stones—stones that are shaped into images and anointed and crowned—when you know that the disgrace of this error redounds no less to you than to him."

With this conversation we had traversed the middle stretch of the city and were now holding to the open shore. There the gentle wave was spreading over the outermost sands, as if it were spreading a carpet for walking, and since the sea is always restless even when the winds are still, even if it did not come out to the land with white and foaming waves, we nevertheless took great delight in its rippling and winding wanderings in that same place, as we dipped our feet at the very edge of the water—the wave now playfully dashing against our feet as it came in, now flowing back and drawing its traces into itself as it receded.

And so, advancing slowly and peacefully, we traced the path of the gently curving shore with stories beguiling the way. These stories were Octavius's account, as he discoursed about navigation. But when we had consumed a sufficiently proper stretch of walking with conversation, we turned our steps back and wore the same path in reverse, and when we came to the place where small boats had been drawn up and were resting on supporting timbers, lifted clear of the earth's stain, we saw boys eagerly competing in a game of throwing potsherds into the sea.

The game is this: they pick up from the shore a potsherd smoothed by the tossing of the waves, take hold of the potsherd flatwise with their fingers, and spin it as low and as close to the water as they can over the waves, so that the missile either skims the sea's back or swims along as it glides with gentle force, or leaps up as it clips the tops of the waves and emerges, lifted by its constant bouncing. The boy whose potsherd ran farthest and skipped most frequently claimed the victory among them.

problems.why: The pagan opponent is called Caecilius in most sections but addressed as Marcus in others, confusing the reader about identity.
problems.fix: Standardize the name to Caecilius or explain that Marcus is his praenomen.

problems.why: Octavius is suddenly called 'Januarius' with no explanation; reader thinks a new person.
problems.fix: Add note: Januarius is an alternate name for Octavius.

problems.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
problems.why: Caecilius is suddenly called 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks a new person.
problems.fix: Add note: Natalis is an alternate name for Caecilius.

problems.quote: With this conversation we had traversed the middle stretch of the city
problems.why: Octavius's quoted speech ends mid-section; narrator resumes without clear marker.
problems.fix: Add closing quotation marks after Octavius's speech.

edits.old: With this conversation we had traversed
edits.new: With this speech of his we had traversed

fixed: The source has 'Marce frater' (vocative of Marcus), so 'my brother Marcus' is correct; no change needed.
The reported problem about 'Januarius' does not appear in this section; no edit needed.
The reported problem about 'Natalis' does not appear in this section; no edit needed.

The source has 'cum hoc sermone eius' ('with this speech of his'), so the English 'With this conversation' loses the reference to Octavius's speech; changed to 'With this speech of his' to mark the narrator's resumption.
